scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Hula Kahiko: Dance of the Sacred Chant
This is Hula kahiko. Pre-1894.
on_screen: Title card: Hula kahiko · USA (Hawaii) · Pre-1894

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Hula kahiko developed in the Hawaiian Islands before Western contact, embodying oral histories through chant and dance.
It predates 1894 and excludes Western instruments.
The dance was integral to religious ceremonies and chiefly entertainment, with strict protocols to avoid errors that could bring misfortune.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Hula kahiko was performed for chiefly entertainment, religious ceremonies, and honoring Hawaiian gods.
It was a form of fealty and spiritual expression.
Performances required flawless execution to avoid bad luck.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Hula kahiko is performed standing (luna) or sitting (noho).
Dancers use complex hand gestures to interpret the mele's words, representing nature and emotions.
Footwork relies on a core set of steps: kāholo, kaʻo, kāwelu, hela, ʻuwehe, and ʻami.
Watch for ʻAmi, Kāholo.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Performed solo or in groups; dancers maintain spacing to allow clear hand gesture visibility; spatial path varies by choreography.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music consists of oli (vocal chant) without melodic instruments, using varied vocal styles such as olioli (melodic) and kepakepa (rapid speech).

Percussion includes the pahu (sacred sharkskin drum), ipu (single gourd drum), ipu heke (double gourd drum), pūniu (small knee drum), ʻiliʻili (lava stone castanets), ʻulīʻulī (feathered gourd rattles), pūʻili (split bamboo sticks), and kālaʻau (rhythm sticks).
Listen for the pahu (sharkskin drum), ipu (single gourd drum), ipu heke (double gourd drum), pūniu (small knee drum).

The sound is dominated by deep, resonant pahu drum beats and hollow, rhythmic ipu percussion, punctuated by sharp ʻiliʻili stones and feathered ʻulīʻulī rattles, underpinning the chanting voice that varies from rapid speech to melodic vibrato.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women traditionally wore pāʻū skirts, sometimes very long and topless historically, adorned with lei made from sacred forest materials.
Men wore malo loincloths and similar adornments.
Costumes and lei were considered sacred and left as offerings after performances.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The kumu hula (master teacher) is central to teaching hula kahiko, guiding students through ritual and technique.
The goddess Laka is revered as the spiritual protector of hula dancers.
Hula kahiko includes various styles such as ʻālaʻapapa, haʻa, and ʻōlapa.
Hula kahiko is the ancestor of modern hula ʻauana, which incorporates Western instruments and influences.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Hula kahiko is child of Hula ʻauana: Modern evolution of hula incorporating Western instruments and melodic songs.
Hula kahiko is variant of Ai Kahiko: 20th and 21st-century hula composed in the ancient kahiko style.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Hula kahiko is performed to oli (chant) which carries mana (spiritual power). The kumu hula (teacher) and students observe strict protocols including ritual permission chants and seclusion during learning to honor the dance's sacred nature.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Women traditionally wore pāʻū skirts, sometimes very long and topless historically, adorned with lei made from sacred forest materials. Men wore malo loincloths and similar adornments. Costumes and lei were considered sacred and left as offerings after performances. Performances took place in hālau (schools) or during ceremonies honoring chiefs or gods, often with ritual seriousness.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Hula kahiko was performed for chiefly entertainment, religious ceremonies, and honoring Hawaiian gods. It was a form of fealty and spiritual expression. Performances required flawless execution to avoid bad luck. Learning dancers were secluded and protected by rituals. Today, it is performed at cultural festivals and hālau, preserving Hawaiian history and spirituality.
